notes:
Now I have substantial material from the key sources. Let me compile the verse-by-verse notes.

---

# Exodus 12:1–26 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## v. 1 — *"Now the LORD said to Moses and Aaron in the land of Egypt…"*

**Traditional Reading:**
- The location is emphasised: this law was given **in Egypt**, not at Sinai — meaning Israel was not lawless before Sinai. The Passover legislation stands apart from the Sinai covenant (Precept Austin, citing Currid). [https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-12-commentary](https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-12-commentary)
- Ellicott notes that Exodus 12:1–28 appears to have been written as part of the **Law rather than the history**, pulling together instructions given at different times (some before the 10th of Abib, some on the day before departure, some after). [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/12.htm](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/12.htm)
- Gill suggests the speech may have occurred on the **first day of the month** (since the lamb was to be taken on the 10th), and the account was placed here to avoid interrupting the plague narrative. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/12.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/12.htm)
- **Wesley** notes that God speaks to both Moses and Aaron, indicating shared leadership in communicating the Passover instructions. [https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/exodus/12.htm](https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/exodus/12.htm)

---

## v. 2 — *"This month is the beginning of months for you; it shall be the first month of your year."*

**Traditional Reading:**
- **David Guzik (Enduring Word):** The coming deliverance was so significant that God told Israel to **remake their calendar** — the new year would start with the month of their redemption. Everything was to change. He quotes G. Campbell Morgan: "God is ever the God of new beginnings in the history of failure," and Spurgeon: "Commence a nation's annals from its evangelization." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-12/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-12/)
- **Ellicott:** Hitherto the Hebrews began the year with **Tishri** (autumnal equinox). Now God made **Abib** (spring, later called Nisan) the first month. Henceforth they had **two years** — a civil year (starting Tishri) and a sacred year (starting Abib). [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/12.htm](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/12.htm)
- **Gill:** This month (Abib/Nisan) became the "chief and principal" of months, famous for the Exodus, and later for the sufferings and death of the Messiah at Passover. Before this, Israel followed the Egyptian calendar with a different beginning. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/12.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/12.htm)
- **Precept Austin (Hobbs):** The Passover provided a **new beginning** for Israel, foreshadowing the new beginning and new life offered to sinners through Christ (2 Cor. 5:17). [https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-12-commentary](https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-12-commentary)
- The month corresponds to **March/April** on the Gregorian calendar. The Hebrew word *rosh* ("beginning") also means "head," conveying not just first but **most prominent**. (Precept Austin) [https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-12-commentary](https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-12-commentary)

**Reformed Perspective:**
- **Ligonier:** In the context of the Passover, God saved Israel not only *from* slavery but also *from* God's own wrath — the blood was a sign that the Israelites, being sinners, deserved death no less than the Egyptians. The lamb died in their place. [https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/saved-god-god](https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/saved-god-god)

**Modern Scholarship:**
- The NET Bible notes that the point was not to make spring the New Year (the autumn New Year already existed), but to make this month the **first in counting months**, because it marked the great festival of freedom. (Precept Austin, citing Jacob) [https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-12-commentary](https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-12-commentary)

---

## v. 3 — *"Tell the whole congregation of Israel that on the tenth day of this month each man must select a lamb for his family…"*

**Traditional Reading:**
- **Guzik:** The lamb was to be taken on the **10th** and kept until the **14th** — four days. This made the lamb **part of the family**; by sacrifice time it was both cherished and mourned. God wanted the sacrifice of something precious. The rabbis later determined at least 10 and not more than 20 persons per lamb. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-12/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-12/)
- **Ellicott:** The four-day gap allowed **ample time for careful inspection** to confirm the animal was without blemish. The word *seh* ("lamb") is a vague term applying to sheep or goats of any age and either sex — sex and age were fixed in v.5. [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/12.htm](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/12.htm)
- **Gill:** The instruction that "every man" take a lamb means every **head of a household**. Jewish tradition held that the four-day selection rule was peculiar to the **first Passover in Egypt only**, not for later generations. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/12.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/12.htm)
- **Wesley:** The lamb was to be got ready four days before, and killed that afternoon as a **religious ceremony**, not strictly a sacrifice on an altar, but acknowledging God's goodness. [https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/exodus/12.htm](https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/exodus/12.htm)
- **Guzik** notes the first use of the term *"congregation of Israel"* (*‘edah*) in the Pentateuch — a technical term describing Israel in its religious sense, underlying the NT use of *ekklesia* ("church") (citing Cole). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-12/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-12/)

---

## v. 4 — *"If the household is too small for a whole lamb, they are to share with the nearest neighbor…"*

**Traditional Reading:**
- **Ellicott:** Where a family was not large enough to consume an entire lamb at one sitting, they were to **club together with neighbours** — either two small families joining, or a large family drafting members to a small one. Josephus says ten was the minimum, twenty not too many. [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/12.htm](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/12.htm)
- **Gill:** The rule was: "count men according to their eating," admitting more or fewer based on consumption. If a man slew the lamb for those who did not eat of it, it was invalid. Gill also sees a **typological foreshadowing** of Gentiles being called to partake of Christ alongside Jews (Eph. 3:5). [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/12.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/12.htm)
- **Guzik:** The sacrifice of Jesus has to be **appropriate to each home**, not simply on a national or community basis — the lamb must fit the household. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-12/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-12/)

---

## v. 5 — *"Your lamb must be an unblemished year-old male, and you may take it from the sheep or the goats."*

**Traditional Reading:**
- **Gill:** The lamb must be **without blemish** — Maimonides listed fifty blemishes that disqualified a sacrifice. This typified Christ: "a lamb without spot and blemish, either of original sin, or actual transgression, holy in his nature, harmless in his life." A **male of the first year** denotes Christ's strength and vigour, His short life among men, and His being tender food for faith. Taking from sheep or goats: the goat's "ill smell" may denote Christ being made sin for His people. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/12.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/12.htm)
- **Ellicott:** Natural piety teaches we must give God of our **best** — not the blind, lame, or sick (Mal. 1:8). A male was fitting because the victim represented the **firstborn male** in each house. "Of the first year" = not above a year old. [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/12.htm](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/12.htm)
- **Guzik:** The Hebrew *seh* applies equally to sheep and goats; the Hebrews, like the Chinese, regarded the distinction as a minor subdivision. The sacrifice had to be **as perfect as a lamb could be**. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-12/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-12/)
- **Reformed (Ligonier):** The unblemished male lamb foreshadows the **true Lamb of God, Jesus Christ**, who was uniquely without blemish (1 Pet. 1:19). [https://learn.ligonier.org/articles/why-institute-lords-supper](https://learn.ligonier.org/articles/why-institute-lords-supper)

---

## v. 6 — *"You must keep it until the fourteenth day of the month, when the whole assembly… will slaughter the animals at twilight."*

**Traditional Reading:**
- **Ellicott:** "Between the two evenings" — there is debate about the exact time. Onkelos and Aben Ezra said the first evening was sunset, the second about an hour later when stars appeared. But Josephus says the actual time of sacrifice was **"from the ninth to the eleventh hour"** (3–5 p.m.), and the phrase came to be reinterpreted as the decline of the sun from zenith to sunset. [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/12.htm](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/12.htm)
- **Gill:** "Between the two evenings" = between the sun beginning to decline (after noon) and its full setting — about the **ninth hour** (3 p.m.). This matches when Christ was crucified (Matt. 27:46). Josephus confirms Passover was slain from the ninth to the eleventh hour. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/12.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/12.htm)
- **Guzik:** Christ came "in the evening of the world," in the "last hour," when all lay buried in darkness — in the eventide of our sin and death (citing Trapp). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-12/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-12/)
- **Wesley:** The lamb was to be killed by the **whole congregation** — Christ suffered at the hands of "the whole multitude" of the Jews (Luke 23:18). [https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/exodus/12.htm](https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/exodus/12.htm)

---

## v. 7 — *"They are to take some of the blood and put it on the sides and tops of the doorframes…"*

**Traditional Reading:**
- **Guzik:** The blood was applied to the **two sides and the top** of the doorway. The only part of the sacrifice given to God was the **blood**; the rest was eaten or burned. The pattern of blood on the two sides and lintel suggests an **abstract shape of a cross**. The blood on the doorposts meant the sacrifice was remembered in daily life — seen every time one went in or out. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-12/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-12/)
- **Precept Austin:** The blood was an **external sign** that those within were numbered among the LORD's people and safe from death. Constable adds that smearing blood on the door with hyssop was an act of **expiation (cleansing)** — the houses of the Israelites were consecrated as altars (they had no other altars in Egypt). The blood was not applied to the **threshold** lest anyone tread on it (cf. Heb. 10:29). [https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-12-commentary](https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-12-commentary)
- **Ellicott:** The word "upper door post" derives from *shacaph*, "to look out," and may refer to a **latticed window above the door** (common in Egyptian houses) through which people could see who knocked. The blood there would be conspicuous, showing atonement had been made for the house. [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/12.htm](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/12.htm)
- **Wesley:** The blood sprinkled on the doorposts typified the **open profession** we make of faith in Christ — "the seal of the lamb is always in the forehead" (Rev. 7:3). If Christ's blood is sprinkled on our consciences, it protects from the wrath of God. [https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/exodus/12.htm](https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/exodus/12.htm)

---

## v. 8 — *"They are to eat the meat that night, roasted over the fire, along with unleavened bread and bitter herbs."*

**Traditional Reading:**
- **Gill:** Roasting was the quickest method (haste was required) and denoted Christ enduring the **wrath of God poured out as fire**. **Unleavened bread** signified sincerity and truth (1 Cor. 5:7–8) in opposition to the leaven of error, hypocrisy, and malice. **Bitter herbs** expressed the bitter afflictions of Egypt, the persecutions believers must expect, and the need for repentance — feeding on a crucified Christ with mourning for sin. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/12.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/12.htm)
- **Ellicott:** Roasting was the simplest, most primitive cooking mode and the only one available to all Hebrews (many would lack cauldrons for a whole lamb). It also distinguished this sacrifice from others (which were often boiled — 1 Sam. 2:14–15). Bitter herbs represented **self-denial or repentance**. [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/12.htm](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/12.htm)
- **Guzik:** The fire represented God's judgment — the lamb came into direct contact with the fire. The bitter herbs accompanied the meal, pointing to the bitter cup Christ drank. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-12/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-12/)
- **Wesley:** The paschal lamb was killed not merely to be looked at but to be **fed upon** — so we must by faith make Christ ours, receive spiritual strength from Him, and have delight in Him as in eating when hungry. [https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/exodus/12.htm](https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/exodus/12.htm)

---

## v. 9 — *"Do not eat any of the meat raw or cooked in boiling water, but only roasted over the fire—its head and legs and inner parts."*

**Traditional Reading:**
- **Gill:** "Raw" (*na*) means **not roasted enough** — flesh on which fire has barely begun to operate. Not boiled at all — showing that Christ is not to be received in a cold, lukewarm manner. Only roasted — and the rabbinic canons describe roasting by transfixing the lamb on a **wooden spit through the mouth to the posteriors**, suspended in a furnace with fire below, so it hung rather than being turned on a spit. **Justin Martyr** (Dialogue with Trypho) says the lamb was roasted in the **form of a cross**: one spit from lower parts to head, another across the shoulders to which the legs were fastened. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/12.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/12.htm)
- **Ellicott:** The lamb was to be roasted **whole** — "not a bone of it was to be broken" (v.46). He also cites Justin Martyr's description of the two wooden spits forming a cross shape. [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/12.htm](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/12.htm)

---

## v. 10 — *"Do not leave any of it until morning… you must burn up any part that is left over."*

**Traditional Reading:**
- **Guzik:** The Passover lamb had to be **eaten completely** — a family had to totally consume the sacrifice. You had to **take it all then**, not store up some rescue for later. "We take all of Jesus, not just the parts that please us." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-12/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-12/)
- **Ellicott:** The remains were to be burned so there could be **neither profanation nor superstitious use** of what was left (comparable to the Church of England's requirement for the Eucharistic elements). The bones and residual flesh were to be annihilated by fire to secure them from profanation. [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/12.htm](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/12.htm)
- **Gill:** A whole Christ is to be received and fed upon by faith. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/12.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/12.htm)
- **Wesley:** God would have them **depend upon Him for daily bread** — they were not to hoard. [https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/exodus/12.htm](https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/exodus/12.htm)

---

## v. 11 — *"This is how you are to eat it: You must be fully dressed for travel… sandals on your feet… staff in your hand. You are to eat in haste; it is the LORD's Passover."*

**Traditional Reading:**
- **Ellicott:** These injunctions were **not repeated in later Law** and were not regarded as binding at any Passover after the first. They all referred to the **impending departure** — long robe girded up, sandals on feet (normally not worn indoors), staff in hand. The meal was eaten "in haste" as liable to be interrupted at any moment by the summons to depart. Christians should similarly maintain a pilgrim attitude, "since they know not when the summons may come to them requiring them to quit the Egypt of this world." The word "Passover" (*pesakh*) occurs here for the first time. [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/12.htm](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/12.htm)
- **Guzik:** The lamb had to be eaten **in faith**, trusting that deliverance was present and that they would walk in it immediately. Hebrews 11:28 says, "By faith he [Moses] kept the Passover." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-12/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-12/)
- **Wesley:** The departing posture signifies that when we feed upon Christ by faith, we must **sit loose to the world** and everything in it. [https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/exodus/12.htm](https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/exodus/12.htm)

---

## v. 12 — *"On that night I will pass through the land of Egypt and strike down every firstborn male… I will execute judgment against all the gods of Egypt. I am the LORD."*

**Traditional Reading:**
- **Guzik:** God regarded Israel as His **firstborn** (Ex. 4:22–23); if Egypt refused to release God's firstborn, God required Egypt's firstborn as penalty. The plague was also directed against specific Egyptian gods — **Osiris** (giver of life) and the supposed deity of **Pharaoh** himself. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-12/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-12/)
- **Ellicott:** "Against all the gods of Egypt I will execute judgment" — the death of firstborn **beasts** was a heavy judgment on Egypt's gods. Many sacred animals were considered incarnations of deity (cows, cats, crocodiles, ibises, etc.). A general destruction of firstborn animals was a blow to the gods. [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/12.htm](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/12.htm)
- **Wesley:** The idols of Egypt were probably **defaced** — metal ones melted, wooden ones consumed, stone ones broken to pieces (Num. 33:4). [https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/exodus/12.htm](https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/exodus/12.htm)

---

## v. 13 — *"The blood on the houses where you are staying will distinguish them; when I see the blood, I will pass over you. No plague will fall on you to destroy you…"*

**Traditional Reading:**
- **Guzik:** The blood was **essential**. An Israelite who didn't apply the blood would still face judgment even if they owned the lamb; an Egyptian who believed and obeyed could be spared. Intellectual agreement was not enough — they had to **actually do** what God said with the blood. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-12/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-12/)
- **Precept Austin:** "When I see the blood, I will pass over you" — it was **not a sign for Pharaoh but for the Israelites**. The sign was a manifestation of God's **grace**, bestowing unmerited favour based on His covenant promises to Abraham. [https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-12-commentary](https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-12-commentary)
- **Ellicott:** "The blood shall be for a token for you" — i.e., a token to **God on Israel's behalf**, not to the Israelites themselves. It distinguished the houses where Israelites dwelt. The translation "pass over" is the emphatic clause from which the lamb and feast derive their name. [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/12.htm](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/12.htm)
- **MacLaren:** The lamb without blemish, chosen and kept for four days until it became "part of the household" and then solemnly slain by the head of the family, was their **representative**. Sprinkling its blood on the posts was an act of **confession, deprecation, and faith** — it accepted the divinely appointed means of safety. [https://www.preceptaustin.org/maclaren_on_exodus](https://www.preceptaustin.org/maclaren_on_exodus)

**Reformed (Ligonier):**
- God did not need the blood-mark to tell Israelites from Egyptians — the sign points to a **deeper theological reality**: judgment was passing indiscriminately; every family deserved death, even the Israelites. Nothing inherent in them made them less worthy of death. The blood signified that **death had already taken place** in that household — judgment had been meted out on a substitute victim. [https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/lords-passover](https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/lords-passover)
- Ligonier also emphasises that Israel was being saved **by God from God** — the firstborn sons of Israel deserved death no less than Egypt's. The lamb's blood symbolically shielded them from God's wrath because the lamb was slain **in their place**, foreshadowing those covered by Christ's blood. [https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/saved-god-god](https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/saved-god-god)

---

## v. 14 — *"And this day will be a memorial for you, and you are to celebrate it as a feast to the LORD, as a permanent statute for the generations to come."*

**Traditional Reading:**
- **Ellicott:** The Passover is **continued in the Eucharist** (1 Cor. 5:7–8); the Church's Easter celebration corresponds in time to the Paschal ceremony and takes its place. Thus the Passover may be regarded as still continuing under Christianity, intended to continue "even to the end of the world." [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/12.htm](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/12.htm)
- **Guzik:** Passover was the **greatest work of redemption** performed on the Old Testament side of the cross — just as Jesus gave the new Passover (Lord's Supper) saying His work on the cross was for all generations (Luke 22:14–20). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-12/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-12/)
- **Pulpit Commentary (Homiletics):** The Passover as an ordinance for later generations was a **guarantee for handing down an ungarbled tradition** of the meaning of the ceremony, taking advantage of children's questions to impress the young (vv. 26–27). [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/exodus/12.htm](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/exodus/12.htm)

---

## v. 15 — *"For seven days you must eat unleavened bread. On the first day you are to remove the leaven from your houses. Whoever eats anything leavened… must be cut off from Israel."*

**Traditional Reading:**
- **Guzik:** Passover began on the 10th; on the **14th** they ate the Passover (the first day of unleavened bread); then for seven days, only unleavened bread. Leaven was a picture of **sin and corruption** — a little leaven influences the whole lump, and leaven "puffs up" as pride does. God called them to walk "unleavened" after deliverance — a life of moral purity. Some suggest a **hygienic** aspect: removing old dough that could harbour harmful bacteria. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-12/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-12/)
- **Ellicott:** "Put away leaven out of your houses" — there was to be **no compromise**, nothing resembling half measures. Leaven as typical of corruption must be wholly put away — a solemn warning against compromise with sin. "Cut off from Israel" means excommunication, perhaps including death. [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/12.htm](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/12.htm)
- **Wesley:** The feast of unleavened bread typified the **Christian life** (1 Cor. 5:7–8). Having received Christ: (1) We must keep a feast in **holy joy**; (2) It must be a feast of unleavened bread — kept in charity, without the leaven of malice, in sincerity, without hypocrisy. All the old leaven of sin must be put far from us. [https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/exodus/12.htm](https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/exodus/12.htm)

---

## v. 16 — *"On the first day you are to hold a sacred assembly, and another on the seventh day. You must not do any work on those days, except to prepare the meals…"*

**Traditional Reading:**
- **Ellicott:** The "holy convocation" was a **general gathering** of the people to the sanctuary for sacrifice, worship, and perhaps instruction (cf. Neh. 8:1). The people were summoned by the blowing of silver trumpets (Num. 10:2). "No manner of work" — or "no servile work" as clarified in Lev. 23:7–8 — was to be done. [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/12.htm](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/12.htm)
- The allowance to **prepare meals** as the only exception shows that the Sabbath principle here is not as strict as later Sabbath law — necessary food preparation was permitted. (Implied in the text itself and Ellicott's notes.)

---

## v. 17 — *"So you are to keep the Feast of Unleavened Bread, for on this very day I brought your divisions out of the land of Egypt… a permanent statute…"*

**Traditional Reading:**
- **Ellicott:** The expression "have I brought" suggests these directions were either **given after the Exodus** or not reduced to writing until then. The word "armies" (or "divisions" in BSB) applied to Israel reflects their organisation as God's hosts. [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/12.htm](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/12.htm)
- **Guzik:** For the first Passover, unleavened bread was a **practical necessity** — they left in such a hurry there was no time for dough to rise. After the first Passover, it was a **testimony** throughout generations. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-12/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-12/)

---

## v. 18 — *"In the first month you are to eat unleavened bread, from the evening of the fourteenth day until the evening of the twenty-first day."*

**Traditional Reading:**
- **Ellicott:** The evening intended is **not** the evening with which the 14th began, but the evening with which it **closed** — the end of the 14th / beginning of the 15th (Lev. 23:5–6). [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/12.htm](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/12.htm)
- This specifies the exact **seven-day window** (14th evening to 21st evening), giving precision to what "seven days" meant and linking the Passover meal (eaten on the night of the 14th/15th) to the week of unleavened bread that followed.

---

## v. 19 — *"For seven days there must be no leaven found in your houses. If anyone eats something leavened… whether a foreigner or native… must be cut off…"*

**Traditional Reading:**
- **Ellicott:** "A stranger" means a **foreigner in blood** who has been adopted into the nation, received circumcision, and become a full proselyte. From the first, it was open to non-Hebrews to share in Hebrew privileges by accepting the covenant of circumcision. "Born in the land" means natives of **Canaan**, regarded as Israel's true home from the time of the first promise (Gen. 12:7). [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/12.htm](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/12.htm)
- The equal application to **foreigner and native** alike shows that God's law applied impartially within the community — no exceptions based on ethnicity for those dwelling among Israel.

---

## v. 20 — *"You are not to eat anything leavened; eat unleavened bread in all your homes."*

**Traditional Reading:**
- This verse serves as the **summary command** wrapping up the Feast of Unleavened Bread instructions — the absolute prohibition on leaven in all dwellings. The emphasis on "in all your homes" (or "habitations") underscores that this was a **domestic, household-level observance**, not merely a sanctuary ritual.

---

## v. 21 — *"Then Moses summoned all the elders of Israel and told them, 'Go at once and select for yourselves a lamb for each family, and slaughter the Passover lamb.'"*

**Traditional Reading:**
- **Ellicott:** Moses had been directed to "speak unto all the congregation" (v.3) but understood the direction as allowing him to do so **mediately, through the elders**. "Draw out" — either "withdraw and take" (intransitive), or "withdraw a lamb from the flock" (transitive). [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/12.htm](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/12.htm)
- **Guzik:** The elders were expected to **lead the way**; Moses instructed them knowing the rest of the nation would follow. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-12/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-12/)
- Moses now communicates the divine instructions to the people, confirming they understood and obeyed — this transitions from the legal section to the historical narrative of what actually happened.

---

## v. 22 — *"Take a cluster of hyssop, dip it into the blood in the basin, and brush the blood on the top and sides of the doorframe. None of you shall go out the door of his house until morning."*

**Traditional Reading:**
- **Ellicott:** The "hyssop" (*ezob*) is probably the **caper plant** (called *asaf* by Arabs), which grows plentifully in the Sinaitic region and was regarded as having **purifying properties** (Lev. 14:4, 49–52; Num. 19:6; Ps. 51:7). The "basin" — the word also means "threshold," causing translation difficulty. The LXX and Jerome preferred "threshold." Moses probably assumed blood was caught in a basin whenever a victim was offered. The command "none of you shall go out" seems to have been given by Moses **on his own authority**, without positive divine direction — he understood that the atoning blood was the sole protection and that outside the sprinkled portal there was **no safety**. [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/12.htm](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/12.htm)
- **Guzik:** Hyssop was always connected with **purification through sacrifice** — used for cleansing lepers (Lev. 14:6), making the water of purification (Num. 19:6, 18). David prayed, "Purge me with hyssop" (Ps. 51:7). Even at the crucifixion, the sponge of sour wine was put on a bunch of hyssop (John 19:29). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-12/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-12/)
- **Wesley:** The blood had to be **sprinkled**, not merely shed — noting the application of Christ's merits to our souls. It was applied to the doorposts, noting the **open profession** we make of faith in Christ. [https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/exodus/12.htm](https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/exodus/12.htm)

---

## v. 23 — *"When the LORD passes through to strike down the Egyptians, He will see the blood… and will pass over that doorway; so He will not allow the destroyer to enter your houses and strike you down."*

**Traditional Reading:**
- **Ellicott:** "The destroyer" (LXX: *τὸν ὀλεθρεύοντα*) — the "plague" of v.13 is here personified. Jehovah appears to have employed an **angel** (or angels, Ps. 78:49) as His agents to effect the actual slaying of the firstborn (cf. 2 Sam. 24:16; 2 Kgs. 19:35). There is no struggle between Jehovah and "the destroyer" — the destroyer is simply His **minister** (Heb. 1:14), bidden to enter some houses and pass over others. [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/12.htm](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/12.htm)
- **Guzik:** The LORD **looked for blood**. Rescue from the angel of death did not come by prayer, fasting, or good works — it was accomplished by a **life given on behalf of others**. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-12/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-12/)
- **Reformed (Ligonier):** The blood distinguished the people of God from unbelieving Egyptians; its application was a **sign of faith**. The Passover marked Israel's redemption from slavery and commemorated her birth as a nation. [https://learn.ligonier.org/articles/why-institute-lords-supper](https://learn.ligonier.org/articles/why-institute-lords-supper)

---

## v. 24 — *"And you are to keep this command as a permanent statute for you and your descendants."*

**Traditional Reading:**
- **Gill:** "This thing" refers not to the sprinkling of blood (peculiar to the Egyptian Passover) but to the **whole observance** — the feast of Passover and unleavened bread with all their rites — to be observed **until the coming of Christ**. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/12.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/12.htm)
- **Ellicott:** "This thing" = the sacrifice of the lamb commanded in v.21, not the blood-sprinkling which was **never repeated** after the first occasion. [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/12.htm](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/12.htm)
- **Guzik:** The deliverance of Passover was not only for that generation but for **all generations to follow**. Just as Jesus gave the new Passover (Lord's Supper), saying His work was for all generations (Luke 22:14–20). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-12/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-12/)

---

## v. 25 — *"When you enter the land that the LORD will give you as He promised, you are to keep this service."*

**Traditional Reading:**
- The instruction looks forward in **faith** to the Promised Land — at the moment of institution, Israel was still in Egypt, yet God speaks with certainty about the land He **will give**. The Passover was to be observed not only in Egypt and the wilderness but in Canaan itself, where the temptation to forget their redemption might be strongest. This verse ties the Passover to the **Abrahamic covenant promise** of the land.

---

## v. 26 — *"When your children ask you, 'What does this service mean to you?'"*

**Traditional Reading:**
- **Guzik:** The Passover was meant to provoke **questions from children** — it was a teaching tool built into the ritual. The answer (v.27) was to be: "It is the Passover sacrifice of the LORD, who passed over the houses of the children of Israel in Egypt…" [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-12/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-12/)
- **Pulpit Commentary (Homiletics):** The Passover observance was connected with **oral instruction** — this was a guarantee for handing down a faithful, ungarbled tradition of the ceremony's meaning; it added to the interest of the service; it took advantage of a favourable opportunity to **impress the minds of the young**; and helped keep alive in all classes a vivid remembrance of God's mighty works. [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/exodus/12.htm](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/exodus/12.htm)
- **Ligonier:** The Passover was to be a **teaching opportunity** for Israelite parents, who were to explain its significance to their children. [https://learn.ligonier.org/articles/why-institute-lords-supper](https://learn.ligonier.org/articles/why-institute-lords-supper)

---

## Summary of Tradition-Specific Emphases

**Reformed (Ligonier):** Strong emphasis on **substitutionary atonement** — the lamb died in place of the firstborn; Israel was being saved *by God from God*; the blood signified that death had already occurred in that household on a substitute victim; there was nothing inherently different about Israelites that made them less deserving of death. [https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/saved-god-god](https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/saved-god-god) | [https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/lords-passover](https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/lords-passover)

**Wesleyan/Methodist (Wesley's Notes):** Emphasis on the Passover as a **religious ceremony** (not strictly a sacrifice on an altar), strongly typological: the lamb typifies Christ in detail (unblemished, male, first year, no broken bones, killed by the whole congregation). Strong focus on **practical application**: eating = feeding on Christ by faith; unleavened bread = the Christian life of sincerity and charity; bitter herbs = brokenness of heart for sin; departing posture = sitting loose to the world. All the old leaven of sin must be put far from us. [https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/exodus/12.htm](https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/exodus/12.htm)

**Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik):** Emphasis on the **dramatic, experiential** aspects: the lamb living with the family for four days so it became cherished; the blood forming the shape of a cross on the door; taking all of Jesus, not just the parts that please us; God arranging circumstances to make obedience necessary. The commentary draws out how the Passover prefigures Jesus in multiple detailed points. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-12/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-12/)

---

## Other Views

**Modern Scholarship (NET Bible notes, cited at Precept Austin):** The purpose of making Abib the "first month" was not to change the New Year (which remained in autumn), but to make it the **first in counting months** because it marked the great festival of freedom. Some scholars have unnecessarily tried to date one New Year earlier than the other. [https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-12-commentary](https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-12-commentary)
